title: Rehearsing at home, first jobs, carnival parades, then bricklaying
summary: The band rehearses in his father's kitchen, plays free for a church celebration, and becomes the American Brass Band for carnival parades. After marriage he turns to bricklaying with his father and railroad work.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: Yes, sir. And I made a crackerjack, if I have to say it myself. I'm not given to post him, but I'm telling you what's a fact. And so, we had, we, we used to rehearse in my daddy's kitchen. He had a very big kitchen, you know, it was, I believe, 20 feet long, by 16 or 18 feet wide. Now, he says, during the winter months, he says, that's where you all live. So he decided to make a big kitchen, you see. And that's where we used to rehearse, at mine, at 3817 Dauphine Street, in my daddy's home. And he used to get a kick out of that, you understand? And he felt that, he was proud to see young fellas, you know, that wanted to take up something like that. So, alright. So the first thing you know, the ancient order of Harbournia is, at the church down there, the St. Vincent de Paul's church, they had a, they used to have a celebration, you understand? So we told Mr. Terlesco, the professor, we told him about it. So he said, well, we're going to get some music, some pieces, that'll answer the purpose for that. So then on the day, I forget just what day they celebrate that, the ancient order of Harbournia, the church day. You understand? So we were rehearsing pieces and we played for them for nothing. You understand? We didn't want anything for it. We were sort of proud to think that we could do something like that. So we played, that was our first offense, plan for the Harbournia, ancient order of Harbournia. So, well, as times went on, then the carnival come along. And Joe Terlesco says, you fellas like to walk plenty? He says, I'll get you a job, plan for the carnival parade. So, alright. The American Brass Band, that's what we named it. And we came along and we, we done very well. So as times went on, some fellas got mad and understand, and he's kind of drifted apart. So when I got married, I, I didn't bother so much with, the only, sometimes fellas would come to me and ask me, didn't I want to go out a while tonight and serenade fellas. So I told him, I said, well, I'll tell you, I don't mind going with you. But I said, I got a time limit. I told him, when 11 o'clock comes, I'm going. I ain't fooling no longer because I'm, I got a wife. And I was learning to trade brick work instead with my daddy. He was a crackerjack brickler. And he made a good one out of me too. Let me, let me tell you that. I didn't borrow no man. I'd milk, I'd milk, everything was known, made out of bricks. I made canning kittles. I made kittles for the, for the butchers to make sausage, cooked sausage in. You understand? They don't have that no more. They had cooked sausage in and a smoke house with a hole in the front where the smoke would be in there. Just one little hole about that square. You understand? Three or four inches square where the smoke could come out. And they used to hang the sausage up there and there on sticks and smoke them. So, oh I, then later on in years, I, I got to, I made a, a copron under Father Prim's church. You understand? He was so well pleased to see that. I was recommended by a man who, that I know my onions. So, he was so well pleased the way I had made that so nice and round. You see, I drawed the, with a, a cornish. I made the, I made the, I made the form and then I set the rails and I drawed that perfect. So he says to me, you a mighty good man at this. I said, yes sir. He says, well, he says, I'm going to see Gunter and I'm going to make Gunter go and see you about building some copons in, in the cemetery. So, when I did go, I told him, I said, I wouldn't build one at a time because I said, I got my brother who works with me. And I said, he's just as good a mechanic as I am. And I said, when I'd be laying bricks, he could be cementing. Or if he'd be laying bricks, I could be drawing a cornish and on them posts and so on. Well, I wouldn't make but five at a time. But I'd done everything that was known to be in line of brickwork. Everything. I built four flue chimneys, I built eight flue chimneys, I built six flue chimneys. I built everything. Then, once I got slack, I used to go work for the Southern Railroad Company. A fellow that knew me, Lacey, he used to work regularly. And he saw me one day and he said, you ain't working? I said, not right now. He said, well, you want to go to work? He said, I can get you done with J.C. Hall, the resident engineer. I said, well, all right. He said, go down and see him. He said, you can see him there pressing the river. And he says, he'll entertain you. So he asked me whether I was a first class man. I said, well, I said, you'll have to ask Mr. Lacey about that. I said, I worked with him. And I said, I never had a wrong word with him. And I said, everything he told me to do, I'd done it to his satisfaction. So he said, well, all right, I'm going to give you a pass now. And he says, tomorrow morning, you're catching number six out of here and you're going up to Lacey. And he was putting up a tank formation then. And from there I went to all the way to Meridian.
